c.tagline: Turks & Caicos' sleepy salt-era capital — Bermudian streets, a wall dive, and winter whales.

taxi.fareNote: Grand Turk has no Uber or ride-hailing; taxis are unmetered with government-set per-person rates by zone — confirm the fare before boarding. Scooters, golf carts, and rental cars are popular alternatives, and traffic drives on the LEFT.

emergency.note: 911 (and 999) reach police, fire, and ambulance across the Turks and Caicos Islands, a British Overseas Territory. English is the official language and the US dollar the currency.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

hood_landmark.Front Street: Front Street Cockburn Town Grand Turk
hood_landmark.Duke Street: Duke Street Cockburn Town Grand Turk

hood_desc: The waterfront historic core of the capital, where 18th- and 19th-century Bermudian buildings line the seafront; home to the Turks & Caicos National Museum in Guinep House, restaurants, and the old salt-era warehouses — the must-see heart of town.

The seafront lane at the south end of the historic core, where almost all of Grand Turk's hotels sit - Osprey Beach Hotel, the Salt Raker Inn and the Turks Head Inne all stand on it, facing Cockburn Town Beach; the compact, walkable base for most visitors.

A quiet stretch of powder sand north of the town centre, fronting the reef wall and rated the island's best swimming and shore-diving beach; lodging here is limited to a handful of beachfront rental villas.
The breezy residential north end of the island, home to the 1852 Grand Turk Lighthouse, wild donkeys, and clifftop views out to Gibbs Cay; a calm, spread-out area away from the town center.

water.note: Desalinated tap water is generally safe, but most visitors drink bottled.

transit.hours: No scheduled public transport; taxis operate on demand and are most plentiful on cruise-ship days.
transit.note: Grand Turk has no public bus or rail network; getting around relies on taxis, rental cars, scooters, and golf carts, plus walking and cycling in the compact old town. Traffic drives on the left.
transit.pay: Pay taxi drivers in cash (US dollars); fares are fixed by zone. Rental cars, scooters, and golf carts are widely available for exploring the island.

car.idp: Not required (US, UK, and Canadian licenses valid up to 3 months); drive on the LEFT

transit.m: Taxi to Cockburn Town (~5-10 min, fixed fare)

tip.r: A 10-15% service charge is often added to hotel and restaurant bills; if not, 15% is standard, and tipping taxis and dive crews is appreciated.

landmarks: Turks and Caicos National Museum (Guinep House)
Housed in one of the island's oldest stone buildings, the national museum showcases the Molasses Reef shipwreck, the hemisphere's oldest excavated European wreck.
Front Street and Duke Street historic district
Bermudian-style colonial houses, salt-merchant mansions, and low stone walls line Grand Turk's oceanfront main streets, a time capsule of the 19th-century salt era.
Grand Turk Lighthouse
Built of cast iron in 1852 and shipped from England, this clifftop lighthouse on the island's northern tip overlooks whale-watching waters each winter.
Governor's Beach
A dazzling stretch of powder-white sand and calm turquoise water beside the governor's residence, framed by casuarina trees and Grand Turk's famous wall diving offshore.
Columbus Landfall National Park
Protecting the crystalline waters along Cockburn Town's shore, this marine park commemorates the disputed claim that Columbus first landed on Grand Turk in 1492.
Her Majesty's Prison
A stark 19th-century island jail, in use until 1994, now open for tours through cellblocks, gallows yard, and stories of pirates and salt-era justice.
Grand Turk Salinas
The shimmering salt pans at the town's center, worked from the 1600s to the 1960s, still attract wading flamingos and recall the industry that built the island.
Gibbs Cay
A tiny uninhabited cay a short boat ride away, where friendly stingrays glide into the shallows to greet visitors on its perfect crescent beach.
St. Thomas' Anglican Church
One of the Turks and Caicos' oldest churches, built by Bermudian salt rakers in the 1820s, stands whitewashed and breezy above the sea.
Pillory Beach
Grand Turk's prettiest strand north of town, with powdery sand, snorkel-friendly reef, and the plaque marking the purported Columbus first-landfall site.

train.note: There is no railway in the Turks and Caicos. Cockburn Town on Grand Turk is reached by small aircraft from Providenciales, which has the international airport, or by cruise ship at the Grand Turk cruise centre.

bus.note: No international coaches and no public bus network - Grand Turk is small and quiet. Taxis meet flights and cruise ships and operate on fixed rates; golf carts and scooters are the usual rental. There is no terminal.

intl.to: South Caicos & Salt Cay (Turks and Caicos Islands) - small inter-island boats

ferry.note: There is no scheduled international ferry from Grand Turk, and no boat link to Providenciales - that connection is by air. The TCI Ferry Service that runs between Providenciales and North Caicos is at the other end of the archipelago. Small local boats reach Salt Cay when weather allows, and dive boats operate as charters along the wall.

half.name: Salt Cay
half.blurb: A tiny, sparsely populated island of old salinas and colonial ruins, reached from Grand Turk by charter flight or boat.

half.name: South Caicos
half.blurb: A former salt-producing island across the Columbus Passage, offering wild coastline, kayaking and quiet beaches.
